qa.a: Lakshmi felt unsettled and guilty, realising Sabina was scared after yesterday's shouting.

qa.q: What small step did Lakshmi take once the pattern was clear?
qa.a: Lakshmi gave Sabina a calm, private job, apologised for shouting and told her she did not have to keep Lakshmi happy.

qa.q: What might the day have been like for Sabina?
qa.a: It may have felt tense and tiring, watching Lakshmi's face all day and trying to stay on her good side to feel safe.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing that a child's sudden, unnatural agreeableness is a fear reaction, restoring calm first and planning next steps later.

passage: The truck outside the school in Kotwa backfired with a bang like a gun. In the one-room classroom, eight-year-old Siddharth leapt up, threw his slate across the floor and shoved the boy beside him off the mat. Then he stood shaking, fists raised, eyes huge. A few children laughed nervously. Rehana, the teacher, did not raise her voice. She moved the other boy to the far side, told the class to start copying the next line, and knelt a little distance from Siddharth. 'Just a truck, Siddharth. You're safe. Sit down when you're ready.' She handed him her steel tumbler of water. His fists slowly opened. The next morning, when he was calm, she sat with him on the step and talked about the shove, and he helped pick up the other boy's scattered chalks.

qa.q: What made the bang outside the school?
qa.a: The truck outside the school backfired.

qa.q: What did Rehana seem to feel as she watched Siddharth shake with raised fists?
qa.a: She seemed steady and calm, and concerned for him, reading his shove as fright rather than naughtiness.

qa.q: Why did Rehana wait until the next morning to talk about the shove?
qa.a: Talking while Siddharth was still frightened would not help; once he was calm he could listen, understand and make amends.

qa.q: How might the boy who was shoved see what happened?
qa.a: He may have felt startled and hurt, and waiting until Siddharth was calm made a real apology more likely.

grounding: Shows a teacher recognising sudden aggression as a stress reaction to a loud bang, putting safety and calm first and discussing consequences the next day.

passage: 'Sorry, sorry, you're right,' Gopika said, before Tenzin had even finished. They were at Tenzin's dining table in Jayanagar, building their chemistry project, and Tenzin had just rewritten Gopika's section for the third time. Gopika had liked her version. She said nothing about it. At home that evening, when her mother asked whether she wanted rice or chapati, she said, 'Whatever's easier, Amma. Sorry.' When her younger brother changed the TV channel, she smiled and gave him the remote. Later Tenzin texted: 'Be honest, which intro do you prefer?' Gopika stared at the screen for a long time. She honestly did not know any more. Every answer she started began with what Tenzin might want to hear. She typed 'Yours is great!' and then, slowly, deleted it. 'I think I liked my first one,' she wrote, her heart thudding.

qa.q: How many times had Tenzin rewritten Gopika's section?
qa.a: For the third time.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling as she stared at Tenzin's text?
qa.a: She felt lost and anxious, unsure what she really thought because every answer began with what Tenzin might want.

qa.q: What small step did Gopika take, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She deleted 'Yours is great!' and wrote that she liked her first intro, a small honest opinion that begins rebuilding her own voice.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see Gopika's constant agreeing?
qa.a: Tenzin may think Gopika really agrees, and so never learns that her ideas are being lost.

grounding: Shows a teenager who apologises and agrees at home and with a friend to avoid friction, keeping things smooth at the cost of knowing her own opinions.

passage:
'Which film, Santosh?'
'Whatever you want. Sorry.'
'Why are you sorry? I asked you.'
'Sorry. I mean, anything's fine.'
Sahil stopped walking. 'That's nine sorries today. I counted. You didn't even want to come to cricket, but you said yes.'
Santosh laughed awkwardly. 'It's easier. At home, when Papa's had a bad day, the whole house goes tight. If I agree with everyone, it stays calm.'
'And here? We're not your Papa.'
'I know. I just... do it everywhere now.'
'Do you even know which film you want?'
Santosh was quiet. 'Honestly? Not really. Sometimes I don't know what I like any more.'
'Then practise on me. Pick. I won't be upset.'
A long pause. 'The space one.'
'See? Nothing exploded.'

qa.q: How many sorries had Sahil counted?
qa.a: Nine sorries today.

qa.q: Why does Santosh keep agreeing, and what does Santosh feel underneath?
qa.a: Santosh is anxious about tension and wants things to stay calm, and it leaves Santosh feeling lost about what to like.

qa.q: What could Santosh try next, building on this conversation?
qa.a: Santosh could keep practising small honest choices with safe friends like Sahil, such as picking a film or saying no to cricket.

qa.q: How is Sahil affected by Santosh's constant agreeing?
qa.a: Sahil feels puzzled and a little shut out, because Sahil wants a friend's real opinion, not an apology.

grounding: Shows a teenager who agrees quickly and says sorry constantly to keep peace at home and with friends, and how it leaves the teen unsure of their own likes.

passage: Looking back, I think I spent most of Class 11 saying yes. Yes to the science stream because everyone said I was good at maths. Yes to the group's plans, the group's jokes, the group's opinion of whoever was not there. If anyone frowned, I apologised, even when I had done nothing. It kept things smooth, and I was proud of being the easy one. Then, at a college fair, a volunteer asked what I actually enjoyed. My mind went empty. My friend Vinita, standing beside me, said quietly, 'You always ask what we think, Nitin. I don't think I've ever heard what you think.' That stung, because it was true. These days I practise small things: choosing where we eat, saying I didn't like a film. My voice shakes sometimes. But I'm slowly finding out who I am.

qa.q: What stream did Nitin say yes to?
qa.a: The science stream.

qa.q: What did Nitin feel when Vinita spoke at the college fair?
qa.a: Nitin felt stung and exposed, because it was true that nobody had heard Nitin's own opinion.

qa.q: What small steps is Nitin taking now?
qa.a: Nitin practises choosing where they eat and saying when a film was not good, even with a shaky voice.

qa.q: How might Vinita have experienced Nitin as a friend during Class 11?
qa.a: Vinita may have found Nitin easy to be with but hard to really know, since Nitin kept every opinion hidden.

grounding: Shows a teenager who agreed and apologised to keep peace, found it kept things smooth but left no sense of self, and begins to recover it.

passage: Okay, so you want the viva story. I'm Lavanya, and I'd been preparing for weeks. I walk in, three examiners, and the first question is easy, about my own project. And my mind goes white. Not nervous, Vandana. Blank. My hands were stuck to the table, my throat locked, and I could hear the clock. Ten seconds felt like ten minutes. Then I remembered something my hostel senior once told me: breathe out longer than you breathe in. So I did, twice. And I just said it: 'Sorry, I've gone blank. Give me a moment.' One examiner nodded and said, 'Take your time.' Saying it out loud somehow loosened everything. The first sentence came, then the next. I passed. Honestly, the naming-it part is what I tell everyone now.

qa.q: How many examiners were in the viva room?
qa.a: Three examiners.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when the blankness hit?
qa.a: Lavanya felt frozen and panicked, with hands stuck, throat locked and every second stretching.

qa.q: Which two things helped Lavanya recover?
qa.a: Breathing out longer than breathing in, and saying out loud that Lavanya had gone blank and needed a moment.

qa.q: What would change if the examiner had said, 'Come on, it's your own project'?
qa.a: Lavanya might have tightened up even more, and the freeze could have lasted longer.

grounding: Shows a young adult freezing in a viva, mind blank and body stiff, and how slowing the breath and naming the moment helps it pass.

passage:
Monday: In the bank interview, the panel asked Tanuja to talk about herself. Her mind went blank. She sat rigid, mouth dry, and finally said, 'I'm... sorry.' She left without finishing her answer and cried at the bus stop.
Thursday: Her friend Akash came over to practise. Each time she froze, he said, 'Stop. Breathe out slowly. Now say what's happening.' She felt silly saying, 'My mind's gone blank,' but after the fourth time, words came back faster.
The next Tuesday: At a second interview, the same blankness hit on a question about teamwork. Tanuja let out a long breath and said, 'Give me a second, I want to answer this properly.' The panel waited. Her shoulders loosened, and she told them about organising her college fest.

qa.q: What question did the panel ask Tanuja on Monday?
qa.a: To talk about herself.

qa.q: How was Tanuja feeling at the bus stop on Monday?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and upset after freezing, and cried.

qa.q: What did the practice with Akash teach Tanuja to do?
qa.a: To breathe out slowly and name what was happening, so the freeze eased instead of taking over.

qa.q: How might Akash have seen his part in her progress?
qa.a: He probably felt glad and proud to see Tanuja's words come back faster each time she practised.

grounding: Shows a young adult freezing under interview pressure and learning over several days to thaw it by slowing the breath and naming the moment.

passage: Nikita, beta, you think I was always this talkative? Let your Chinmay Mama tell you something. When I was twenty-one, I told my father I wanted to leave engineering. He shouted, 'After all we've spent?' and I stood in the doorway, mouth dry, not a single word in my head. I had rehearsed for days, and it all vanished. My legs felt like wood. My father took my silence as agreement and walked away. For a month I said nothing more. Then one evening I tried again, and when the blankness came, I said, 'Baba, my mind has gone empty. Give me a few minutes.' I went to the balcony and breathed out slowly, again and again. When I came back, I could speak. He didn't agree that night. But he listened.

qa.q: How old was Chinmay when he told his father he wanted to leave engineering?
qa.a: Twenty-one.

qa.q: What was young Chinmay feeling as he stood in the doorway?
qa.a: He felt frozen and overwhelmed; the shouting made his rehearsed words vanish and his legs feel like wood.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chinmay's story?
qa.a: The evening he named the blankness aloud, asked for a few minutes and breathed slowly on the balcony before speaking again.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's father have understood the first silence?
qa.a: He took it as agreement, not realising his son had frozen under the shouting.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a young adult freezing in a heated argument and learning to thaw it by naming the moment and slowing the breath.

passage:
Subject: About yesterday
Hi Shreya,
I've been thinking about the release meeting since yesterday. When I asked about the test results, you said, 'Just do your job and stop asking me things.' Honestly, it stung. I went back to my desk feeling like I'd done something stupid in front of everyone, and my first thought was to go to our manager. But then I remembered you'd been here past midnight three nights running, and that the client had moved the deadline again. I don't think that reply was really about me. I'd still like to talk it over, calmly, once the release is out. Maybe Friday over chai? I want us to work well together, and I'd rather understand what was going on than stay annoyed.
Darshan

qa.q: What did Shreya say when Darshan asked about the test results?
qa.a: 'Just do your job and stop asking me things.'

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after the release meeting?
qa.a: Darshan felt stung and embarrassed, as if having done something stupid in front of everyone.

qa.q: What makes Darshan's email a wise next step?
qa.a: It is honest about the hurt, links the reply to the late nights and deadline pressure, and proposes a calm talk after the release rather than escalating straight away.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Shreya might feel embarrassed about snapping but relieved to be offered understanding and a calmer conversation.

grounding: Shows a coworker who feels attacked by a stressed teammate's sharp reply, then recognises it came from pressure rather than contempt and suggests a calmer talk later.

passage: You know me, yaar, I'm Gurleen, I don't cry at work. But on Tuesday I did, in the stairwell. We had the client presentation at four, and at three-thirty Karthik looked at my slides and said, loudly, 'Did you even check these numbers? Unbelievable.' The whole team heard. My face went red and I thought, fine, he thinks I'm useless. I wanted to never speak to him again. Then, sitting on those stairs, I remembered him telling me last week that this account was his first big chance and he was terrified of losing it. So on Wednesday I waited till lunch was over and said, 'Yesterday really stung. Can we talk about it?' He went pale and said, 'I was panicking. It wasn't about you. I'm sorry.' We fixed the numbers together after that.

qa.q: What time was the client presentation?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel after Karthik's comment in front of the team?
qa.a: Gurleen felt humiliated and hurt, sure Karthik thought Gurleen useless, and wanted never to speak to him again.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen wait until Wednesday to raise it?
qa.a: Waiting until the pressure had passed let both of them speak calmly instead of reacting in the heat of the deadline.

qa.q: How did Karthik seem to see his own comment afterwards?
qa.a: He seemed ashamed, going pale and explaining that he had been panicking, not judging Gurleen.

grounding: Shows a coworker hurt by a stressed colleague's sharp remark who realises it came from fear rather than contempt, making a calmer talk possible the next day.

passage:
Monday: Leela, three weeks into the finance team, asked Chandrika where the audit files were. Chandrika didn't look up. 'Not now! Can't you see I'm drowning?' Leela went back to her seat with burning cheeks and typed half a complaint to HR before deleting it.
Wednesday: Leela noticed Chandrika eating lunch at her desk with shaking hands, phone pressed to her ear, saying, 'Yes, sir. Yes, by Friday. I know what's at stake.' Leela's anger cooled into something closer to worry.
Friday: After the quarter-end files went in, Leela brought two coffees over. Chandrika rubbed her eyes. 'About Monday. I was scared of missing the deadline and I took it out on you. I'm sorry.' They agreed that next quarter, Chandrika would put a red sticky note on her monitor on bad days, and Leela would send questions by message instead.

qa.q: What did Chandrika say when Leela asked about the audit files?
qa.a: 'Not now! Can't you see I'm drowning?'

qa.q: What did Leela feel on Monday, and how did it change by Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday she felt hurt and angry enough to start a complaint; by Wednesday her anger cooled into worry when she saw Chandrika's pressure.

qa.q: What arrangement did they make, and why is it useful?
qa.a: A red sticky note on bad days and questions by message, which lets Leela avoid being snapped at and Chandrika keep focus.

qa.q: How does Chandrika seem to see her Monday reply looking back?
qa.a: She sees it as fear about the deadline spilling out on Leela, and she feels sorry for it.

grounding: Shows a coworker who feels attacked by a stressed teammate's sharp reply, then recognises it came from fear rather than contempt, leading to a calmer later conversation.
